problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts for defects using cameras on 40 lines across three plants. Each line has two to four cameras attached to an ARM edge computer with a small neural accelerator. Plant networks can be unavailable for days. Inspectors label about 5,000 defect images each week, and the model is retrained weekly and pushed to devices. The team has two ML engineers and one half-time operations person, with a tight infrastructure budget.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

points.description: The system packages models into deployed edge modules for on-device inference. On a recurring schedule, training runs on a larger machine; versioned artifacts feed automated progressive releases, with rollback available if a deployed version causes problems. Trade-off: This gains local inference and controlled, reproducible releases, while scheduled retraining provides predictable operations. It gives up responsiveness to unscheduled data or quality changes, and vertically scaling training limits expansion compared with distributing workloads across machines.

1. Models are trained with horizontally or vertically scalable compute, governed through versioned datasets, experiments, artifacts, metadata, and health records. Repository commits trigger staged builds and deployments to edge modules, while production observations and new data feed an automated retraining pipeline. 2. Trade-off: This provides reproducible, scalable delivery and rapid adaptation while keeping inference near devices. It increases operational complexity, compute and release-management costs, and introduces risks from automated retraining and deploying updated models across distributed edge hardware.

The system packages the model as a real-time service integrated with applications, tracking model artifacts and dependencies under version control. Training runs on increasingly larger machines, while environment-gated automation validates and approves releases; practitioners manually initiate retraining when needed. Trade-off: This provides reproducible artifacts, controlled promotion, and straightforward service integration, but vertical scaling limits training capacity and manual retraining slows response to changing data or quality. The approach also depends on increasingly powerful single machines rather than distributed training.

The system packages ONNX-optimized models into deployed edge modules for local inference. Training runs on progressively larger machines, with end-to-end versioning of data, experiments, artifacts, metadata, and health; retraining occurs on a schedule, and updates are released incrementally with rollback capability. Trade-off: This combines local performance and reduced runtime dependence with governed reproducibility and safer releases. It gives up responsiveness to unscheduled data or quality changes, while vertical scaling can limit training capacity and ONNX conversion may constrain some model or runtime features.

The system runs versioned models on deployed edge modules, with retraining initiated on a recurring schedule. Horizontally and vertically scalable training produces governed, reproducible artifacts, while progressive release automation deploys updates incrementally and supports rollback when needed. Trade-off: This gains operational control, reproducibility, scalable training, and resilient releases without requiring continuous retraining. It gives up responsiveness to unscheduled data or quality changes, and edge placement may constrain available compute and complicate coordinated updates across devices.

The system packages ONNX-optimized models into deployed edge modules for local inference. Scheduled retraining runs on a larger machine, while unified automation tests and releases models and services, with version-controlled artifacts supporting reproducibility. Trade-off: This gains automated, performant edge delivery and governed reuse, but scheduled retraining may respond slowly to data changes, and vertical scaling limits training growth to a single larger machine. ONNX conversion and unified releases may also constrain runtime or change-management flexibility.

The system deploys ONNX-optimized models to edge modules for efficient on-device inference, while horizontally or vertically scalable training pipelines produce updates. End-to-end lifecycle governance versions datasets, experiments, artifacts, metadata, and health, and scheduled retraining feeds progressively released updates with rollback capability. Trade-off: This gains efficient, reproducible edge operations and safer releases, but scheduled retraining may respond slowly to sudden data or quality changes. ONNX conversion and comprehensive governance also add implementation and maintenance overhead.

The system packages version-controlled models as ONNX artifacts and deploys them for optimized inference in edge modules. Unified release automation builds, tests, and releases the model and surrounding services, while horizontally or vertically scalable training supports scheduled daily, weekly, or monthly retraining. Trade-off: This gains reproducible releases, improved edge inference performance, and adaptable training capacity, but scheduled retraining may react slowly to sudden data or quality changes. ONNX conversion and on-device placement can also constrain runtime compatibility and available computational resources.

1. Models are converted to ONNX and deployed for inference in edge modules, while training runs on increasingly larger machines and produces version-controlled artifacts. Scheduled retraining creates new artifact versions, which progressive release automation introduces incrementally and can roll back if problems arise. 2. Trade-off: This gains faster, locally executed inference with reproducible releases and recovery, but scheduled retraining may react slowly to changing data, vertical training limits scale to one machine, and edge deployment adds resource constraints.

approaches.idea: What if local inference and progressive rollback anchor the design, with scheduled training and complete lifecycle records?
What if automated staged delivery adapts to new production data, with scalable training and lifecycle governance?
What if a real-time model service centralizes serving and human-triggered training?
approaches.dropped_because: Central model service placement fails the core fit for low-latency inspection during plant network outages; changing retraining or release choices cannot fix that placement conflict.

approaches.idea: What if one unified release process and a compact artifact record keep the edge design easier to operate?

trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping inference on each line should meet R1 and support Q1 and Q2 without depending on the plant network. Weekly scheduling and rollback-oriented release should support R2 and Q3; single-machine training and basic artifact versioning should limit operational burden, though exact targets remain unproven.

tradeoffs.note: A simpler single-machine training path may reduce operational coordination but gives less room to scale the weekly training workload.
A predictable schedule simplifies operations and weekly retraining, while it does not define selection and collection of uncertain or incorrect images.

trajectory.observation: The point checker found no conflicting values or unmet relations, but no source attests the full combination. Edge placement fits the outage and response context; the space does not establish the numeric latency, rollback, or spending targets.

trajectory.hypothesis: Edge serving should protect R1 and Q2, while automatic retraining on incoming labeled data and commit-triggered staged releases should help R2 and Q3. Scalable training and end-to-end governance should accommodate growth but may strain C1 and Q4.

tradeoffs.note: Scalable compute and complete lifecycle records support repeatable delivery, with added platform and maintenance cost for a small team.

alternatives.name: Governed edge with progressive rollback
alternatives.summary: Run optimized models on the installed edge devices, retrain weekly, and use lifecycle governance with progressive deployment and rollback. This favors safe, reproducible updates but asks more of the small operating team.

choices.reason: Local inference avoids a network round trip and uses the installed edge computers; it is the closest available fit to line latency and outage continuity.
ONNX conversion is intended to improve inference performance, subject to testing on the fixed ARM accelerator.
choices.fit_note: The value does not establish a 200 ms bound or compatibility with this device's accelerator.

choices.reason: Progressive rollout and prior-version restoration align with deployment and operator recovery needs, while automation can reduce repeated manual work.

adrs.title: Where to run production inspection
adrs.context: Every part needs an immediate decision, and a plant may lose network access for a week. The installed ARM edge computers are fixed for the year. Local inference is the closest match to these needs; ONNX optimization may help performance, but neither the space nor this study proves the latency target or accelerator compatibility.

options.name: ONNX optimized edge inference
pros: Keeps inference beside the camera during network outages.
Uses the installed edge placement and an optimization intended to improve runtime performance.
cons: Needs measurement against the 200 ms target.
ONNX support on the installed accelerator is not established.
options.reason: All surviving alternatives keep inference local, a pattern described in Composing Deep-Learning Microservices for the Hybrid Internet of Things; Three Levels of ML Software describes ONNX optimization as a performance aid, so it remains a testable choice.

adrs.title: How to retrain and release weekly models
adrs.context: The team needs weekly training from new labels and rollout across many lines, with quick recovery and limited operating capacity and spend. Scheduled retraining matches the cadence, while the release and versioning options vary in recovery support, traceability, and operational scope. The design space does not quantify delivery times or costs, and it does not directly specify uncertainty sampling or durable image collection.

options.name: Governed weekly progressive release
pros: Aligns retraining with a weekly cadence.
Combines flexible training capacity, lifecycle traceability, and rollback-capable progressive delivery.
cons: Comprehensive governance and flexible infrastructure add operating scope.
No value promises the required time or cost bounds.
options.reason: This favors reproducible, recoverable delivery where release risk matters most, accepting more maintenance work. MLOps Principles discusses scheduled retraining; MLOps: Model management, deployment, and monitoring with Azure Machine Learning describes rollback and lifecycle governance.

options.reason: This keeps the release recovery feature while reducing training and governance complexity.
